entries.clue: Cocaine turned up on cheese with this? (7)

annotation.definitionNote: The setter names the answer by what it is eaten with rather than by a synonym, so the definition is a phrase where a noun would normally stand; the question mark is the licence for that.

indicatorNotes.turned up: Something turned up has been tipped back the way it came, and in a down entry that means reading the letters from the foot of the piece upward.

blocks.note: crack is the smokable form of the drug
on in the sense of about is the crossword's RE, stood on its head by the instruction

annotation.surface: A line of cocaine appearing beside the cheese course.
annotation.walkthrough: On is one of the crossword's smallest conventions: it means about, which is written RE. The drug word is doing honest work here, which is rarer in the Eye than it looks.
annotation.definitionFit: Crackers are the dry biscuits a cheeseboard comes with, so the answer is named by its companion on the plate.

entries.clue: Sex at first has the power to examine (4)

indicatorNotes.at first: What comes at first is the opening of the word, so only its leading letter is wanted.

blocks.note: the leading letter of the word, taken as instructed
whoever has the power to do a thing can do it

annotation.surface: Sex, put first, gives someone the authority to look closely.
annotation.walkthrough: Three words of the clue collapse into one short one, which is why the sentence reads so smoothly and gives so little away. Sex is here for its first letter and nothing else.
annotation.definitionFit: To scan something is to run your eye searchingly over it, which is examining it in both the medical and the everyday sense.

entries.clue: Insult Conservative circle (4)

blocks.note: to dis someone is to insult them, the street shortening of disrespect
c is the standing abbreviation for the party

annotation.surface: Hurling abuse at a gathering of Conservatives.
annotation.walkthrough: Circle reads as a set of people keeping company and means a shape. Nothing joins the two pieces at all, which is what makes a four-letter clue this bare.
annotation.definitionFit: A disc is a flat round plate, so the clue names it by its outline — the round shape is the whole of what the word says.

entries.clue: Fancy getting a rise – about $1000, sir? (6)

indicatorNotes.getting a rise: Something getting a rise is travelling upward, and a down entry read upward gives its letters back to front.
indicatorNotes.about: What is about a thing is wrapped round it, so the letters just turned split to take the next piece.

blocks.note: to fancy that something is so is to think it, and the word is then read upward
a grand is a thousand dollars, written G

annotation.surface: Wondering whether a pay rise might come to about a thousand dollars, sir.
annotation.walkthrough: Fancy looks like the clue's tone and is a plain verb meaning think. The Eye's other meaning of getting a rise is there for the surface alone; the instruction is the ordinary one about direction.
annotation.definitionFit: A knight is entitled to Sir before his name, so the form of address stands in for the rank that earns it.

entries.clue: At present the Tories' reduced work situation (10)

annotation.definitionNote: The Tories are plural and name a party, while the answer is the single role they collectively occupy in the Commons — and it is only theirs for as long as they are out of office.

indicatorNotes.reduced: A word that has been reduced is written in less space than usual, which for a word with a standard short form means that short form.

blocks.note: op. is the printed short form of opus, a composer's numbered work
the position someone is in is their situation

annotation.surface: The Tories going into the present with rather less work to do.
annotation.walkthrough: Work situation reads as one phrase about employment and is two separate pieces. The definition dates itself: it holds only while that party sits on the far side of the Commons.
annotation.definitionFit: The Opposition is Parliament's name for the largest party not in government, a role the Conservatives took over after losing the 2024 election.

entries.clue: Presidential period, say, that is restricting Trump's no.1 tree destroyer! (7)

indicatorNotes.say: Say means for instance, marking the words before it as one case of the piece wanted rather than an exact synonym for it.
indicatorNotes.restricting: To restrict something is to close round it and hold it in, so the letters named shut on both sides of the next piece.
indicatorNotes.no.1: A person's no.1 is the one at the front, so the letter wanted is the one the name starts with.

blocks.note: the fixed spell a president serves
i.e. is the Latin id est, which translates as that is
the letter the name starts with, taken as instructed

annotation.surface: Trump's spell in office, and what it is doing to the forests.
annotation.walkthrough: I.e. turns up in crosswords as often for its two letters as for its meaning, and here it is the container rather than the definer. The exclamation mark is flagging a definition that stretches: the damage is done to timber more than to living trees.
annotation.definitionFit: Termites eat their way through wood, hollowing out standing trees and anything sawn from them, so the clue names them by the damage.

entries.clue: Member – objectionable type (5)

blocks.note: the polite anatomical word, not the one on a club's roll
the insult the same word turned into

annotation.surface: Introducing a member of the club who is also a thoroughly nasty piece of work.
annotation.walkthrough: A dash is all the joining there is, and in a clue this short that almost always means two definitions stand either side of it. The second one grew out of the first, which is why they share a word.
annotation.definitionFit: Member is the polite word for the penis, and calling a man a prick is the insult drawn straight from that sense — both are everyday slang.

entries.clue: Slept around and, sadly, taken by force (9)

indicatorNotes.around: To go around something is to pass on both sides of it, so the word named splits and the next piece sits in the gap.
indicatorNotes.sadly: A thing in a sad state has fallen out of the shape it should be in, and letters in that state come out in no order of their own.

blocks.note: to kip is British slang for to sleep, and the word parts after its second letter
the three letters of the word in another order

annotation.surface: A history of sleeping around that ended, sadly, in abduction.
annotation.walkthrough: Kip is British slang for sleep, so Slept wants six letters here rather than the four of a nap. Sadly sits between two commas where it looks like a comment on the story, and it is the instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: Someone kidnapped has been seized and carried off against their will, which is what taken by force describes.

entries.clue: (& 11ac.) What we get from Rachel Reeves is logic? Come on, stupid – zero optimism ultimately! (8)

annotation.definition: What we get from Rachel Reeves

indicatorNotes.stupid: Something stupid has been put together without sense, and letters assembled without sense keep none of the order they came in.
indicatorNotes.ultimately: What happens ultimately happens at the very end, so the letter wanted is the one the word finishes on.

blocks.note: eleven letters of fodder, the question mark and comma read straight through
zero is written as a ring, the same shape as the letter
the letter the word ends on, taken as instructed

annotation.surface: Someone shouting down the Chancellor's reasoning and running out of hope altogether.
annotation.walkthrough: Rachel Reeves is the Chancellor of the Exchequer, Britain's finance minister, so the definition is a verdict on her Budgets. Stupid is both the insult the sentence throws and the instruction the wordplay needs, and the answer runs 9 then 11.
annotation.definitionFit: Economic gloom is the flat, pessimistic outlook a Chancellor's figures leave behind, and the current Chancellor's Budgets have been reported that way throughout.

entries.clue: A Spice Girl performing 'Tit'? (5)

blocks.note: Mel B and Mel C were two of the five Spice Girls
a show being performed is on

annotation.surface: A Spice Girl on stage working through a number called 'Tit'.
annotation.walkthrough: The quotation marks make the last word look like a song title, which is where the definition is hiding. Two singers shared the name, so the clue can say a Spice Girl without naming which.
annotation.definitionFit: Melons has been slang for a woman's breasts for decades, and tit is the coarse word for the same thing, the question mark marking the register.

entries.clue: see 9ac.
Sketch of  Republican outcast almost imitating liberal sources (6)

indicatorNotes.almost: A word given almost in full stops just short of its end, so its last letter is left off.
indicatorNotes.sources: A source is where something starts, and the plural says each of the words that follow is tapped for its starting letter.

blocks.note: Mike Pence, Trump's vice-president, cast out of the movement for certifying the 2020 result, with his last letter docked
the starting letter of each word, taken as instructed

annotation.surface: A drawing of a cast-out Republican done in the manner of the liberal press.
annotation.walkthrough: Imitating reads as the drawing's style and is really two letters' worth of raw material. The surname is one letter longer than the clue lets you keep, which is the whole of the deletion.
annotation.definitionFit: To pencil something is to draw it in soft grey lines, the rough first version an artist puts down, which is what sketch asks for as a verb.

entries.clue: How's your father's platonic love arrangement around university? (10)

indicatorNotes.arrangement: An arrangement is a set of things put in an order somebody chose, so these letters are redealt rather than kept as printed.
indicatorNotes.around: What sits around a thing encloses it, so the redealt letters part and the next one goes between them.

blocks.note: eight letters of fodder, the word taken whole
love is the tennis scoreboard's nothing, written as a ring
u is the short form of university

annotation.surface: A chaste friendship rearranged around a university.
annotation.walkthrough: How's your father is British seaside slang for sex, the sort of euphemism the Eye prints instead of the word. Platonic love is what the joke turns on, since platonic love is the one kind that rules the answer out.
annotation.definitionFit: How's your father is the British euphemism for going to bed with someone, and copulation is the clinical noun for the same act.

entries.clue: How right-wing flag hoisters view themselves? Weapons of war (8)

annotation.definition: How right-wing flag hoisters view themselves?

blocks.clueFragment: How right-wing flag hoisters view themselves?
blocks.note: the name the flag-flyers award themselves, which the clue carefully does not endorse
the Patriot is the American surface-to-air missile battery

annotation.surface: Men stringing up flags and thinking well of themselves, next to the hardware of war.
annotation.walkthrough: Flag hoisters is the Eye's phrase for the crowd who fly the St George's cross from lampposts. Weapons of war looks like a second dig at them and is a straight definition, because the missile carries the name.
annotation.definitionFit: People who fly flags call themselves patriots as a badge of loyalty, while the Patriot is also an American missile system, so both halves land on the one word.

entries.clue: Hypocritical Trump's ultimate debts (5)

indicatorNotes.ultimate: A person's ultimate letter is the one their name finishes on, the last of the run.

blocks.note: the letter the name ends on, taken as instructed
an IOU is the scribbled note that stands for a debt

annotation.surface: A hypocrite left holding the last of Trump's debts.
annotation.walkthrough: Trump's ultimate reads as his final ambition and asks only for a letter. The definition works because the word long ago picked up a sneer: virtue worn for display rather than the devout kind.
annotation.definitionFit: Pious describes godliness put on for show, the sanctimonious sort that does not survive inspection, which is how hypocritical reaches it.

entries.clue: Posh prisons– dodgy finance (11)

indicatorNotes.dodgy: Something dodgy is not what it should be, and letters that are not as they should be have left their printed order.

blocks.note: eleven letters, the two words redealt together

annotation.surface: Upmarket jails paid for with shady money.
annotation.walkthrough: Posh prisons is the Eye's dig at the open jails white-collar convicts are sent to, and the phrase is fodder rather than comment. Dodgy reads as a verdict on the money and is the instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: Sponsorship is money put up by a backer in return for a name on the shirt, so finance names it by what it supplies.

entries.clue: Clobbers clobber (5)

annotation.definitionNote: Clobber is a mass noun for clothes and kit, so it names the class the answer belongs to rather than agreeing with it in number.

blocks.note: the verb, meaning to hit someone hard
the noun, British slang for clothes and gear

annotation.surface: Someone laying into a heap of another man's gear.
annotation.walkthrough: Clobber is British slang for clothes and kit, and to clobber is to thump, so the setter gets a whole clue out of one word used twice. The first is a verb, the second a noun.
annotation.definitionFit: To sock someone is to hit them, and socks are part of anyone's clobber — the clothes-and-gear sense the word carries in Britain.

entries.clue: University unyielding about endless change (7)

indicatorNotes.about: What is set about something is wrapped round it, so the word named splits to take the next piece.
indicatorNotes.endless: A word made endless has had its end taken off, so the last letter goes.

blocks.note: someone unyielding is hard, and the word parts after its third letter
to change is to vary, docked of its last letter as instructed

annotation.surface: Standing firm about a change that goes on with no end to it.
annotation.walkthrough: University is the crossword's stock single letter nine times out of ten, and here it is the definition — that swap is the trap. Harvard is the oldest university in the United States, founded in 1636.
annotation.definitionFit: Harvard is one particular American university, so the clue defines it by its kind, an example standing in for the general word.

entries.clue: Decline having an erection, being reactionary (7)

blocks.note: a light or an empire that declines dies away
the state the Eye is describing, in one word

annotation.surface: Losing interest at exactly the moment things were looking up.
annotation.walkthrough: Decline is the fading sense of the verb, as a light dies, not the refusing sense. Both halves carry the Eye's second meaning, and the two pieces sit in the order the clue prints them.
annotation.definitionFit: A diehard clings to a position everyone else has given up, which is what reactionary names in politics.

entries.clue: Wads? Roll out the legal team! (3,5)

indicatorNotes.out: Letters that are out are out of their proper order, the way a drawer that is out of order holds nothing where it should be.

blocks.note: four letters of fodder
four more, the two words shuffled together

annotation.surface: Bundles of cash, and a shout to bring the lawyers on.
annotation.walkthrough: The Law Lords were the dozen senior judges who sat in the House of Lords as Britain's final court of appeal, until the Supreme Court replaced them in 2009. Roll out reads as one phrase and hands over only its second word.
annotation.definitionFit: The Law Lords sat together as the country's highest court, so legal team is a breezy way of naming a bench of judges.

entries.clue: Put new lead in your pencil? Terrible ordeal! (6)

annotation.definition: Put new lead in your pencil?

indicatorNotes.Terrible: A terrible version of a thing is a botched one, and letters botched come out in an order nobody intended.

blocks.note: six letters of fodder, redealt

annotation.surface: Putting fresh lead in a pencil after a thoroughly bad experience.
annotation.walkthrough: Lead in your pencil is the old British phrase for sexual vigour, which is the joke the definition carries. A propelling pencil really does take a new lead, and that is what makes it fair.
annotation.definitionFit: To reload is to put a fresh charge into something that has been emptied, which covers the propelling pencil and the innuendo alike.

entries.clue: Jail worked for Frank (6)

blocks.note: the can is American slang for prison
whoever did the work worked

annotation.surface: A spell inside that turned out well for a man named Frank.
annotation.walkthrough: The capital letter mid-sentence makes the last word a man's name, and it is the adjective, lower case anywhere else. Can is the American prison, not the British nick.
annotation.definitionFit: Someone candid says what they think without dressing it up, which is exactly what being frank means.

entries.clue: Critical of Trump initially (showing little bottle on the outside) (5)

indicatorNotes.initially: What comes initially comes at the start, so the letter wanted is the one the name opens with.
indicatorNotes.on the outside: A thing on the outside is wrapped round what is within, so these letters part and the other one goes between them.

blocks.note: a vial is the small glass bottle a chemist uses, and it parts after its second letter
the letter the name opens with, taken as instructed

annotation.surface: Attacking Trump from the outset, with not much courage on display.
annotation.walkthrough: Bottle is British slang for nerve, so showing little bottle reads as cowardice and means a small glass container. The bracket parks the wordplay out of the sentence's way without breaking it.
annotation.definitionFit: Something vital is critical in the sense of being essential to the outcome, the do-or-die sense of the word rather than the fault-finding one.

entries.clue: Artwork? It's cheap crap! (8)

indicatorNotes.crap: Calling a thing crap says it has been thrown together anyhow, and letters thrown together keep no order of their own.

blocks.note: eight letters of fodder, the apostrophe read through

annotation.surface: Dismissing someone's art as cheap rubbish.
annotation.walkthrough: Crap is the verdict the sentence delivers and the instruction the wordplay needs. A pastiche is openly built out of other people's styles, so the insult lands closer to the definition than the setter admits.
annotation.definitionFit: A pastiche is a work knowingly assembled from other artists' manners, so artwork names it by the class it belongs to.

entries.clue: Convention sounds crowded (4)

indicatorNotes.sounds: Sounds asks for the noise the word makes rather than its spelling, so what is wanted is written the way you hear it.

blocks.note: a crowded hall is packed, and said aloud that word spells another

annotation.surface: A convention with the halls full to bursting.
annotation.walkthrough: Convention is the conference in the sentence and the agreement in the answer, the two senses pulling opposite ways. One consonant cluster is all that separates the sound from the spelling.
annotation.definitionFit: A pact is a formal agreement between parties, which is the sense of convention that means a treaty rather than a gathering.

entries.clue: Shit! China's hoarding yen! (4)

indicatorNotes.hoarding: Whoever is hoarding something is keeping it inside, so the letters wanted are sitting within the words already given.

blocks.note: four letters running straight on across the exclamation mark and the space

annotation.surface: An outburst at China stockpiling the Japanese currency.
annotation.walkthrough: Yen is the currency in the sentence and a craving in the definition, which is the whole of the misdirection. The exclamation mark is there to stop the eye running two words together.
annotation.definitionFit: A yen for something is a nagging want you cannot put down, and an itch is the same restless craving.

entries.clue: Dicky or Reagan, harbouring Conservative contempt (9)

indicatorNotes.Dicky: Dicky is British slang for shaky or unsound — a dicky heart — and a shaky set of letters will not stand in the order it was given.
indicatorNotes.harbouring: To harbour someone is to shelter them inside, so the letters just redealt close round the next one.

blocks.note: eight letters of fodder, the two words taken together
c is the standing abbreviation for the party

annotation.surface: A shaky Nixon or Reagan giving shelter to a Conservative.
annotation.walkthrough: Dicky doubles as the Nixon the surface wants standing beside Reagan, which is why two Republican presidents seem to be in the clue. Harbouring says the party letter goes inside rather than alongside.
annotation.definitionFit: Arrogance is self-importance worn as a sneer at everyone else, and that looking-down-the-nose is the contempt the clue means.

entries.clue: Manage to shag Mark (5)

blocks.note: the conquest sense, the one the surface walks straight out of
the notch cut into a tally stick, and the verb for cutting it

annotation.surface: Getting lucky with a man called Mark.
annotation.walkthrough: The capital on the last word makes it a name, and it is a plain verb. Cutting notches in a tally stick is also how the same word came to mean twenty.
annotation.definitionFit: To score is to succeed in pulling someone, and to score a surface is to mark it with a cut or a line — two everyday senses of one verb.
